'''Pallanganmiddang''' (Waywurru, Waveroo) is an extinct, poorly-attested Aboriginal language of the Upper Murray region of the northeast of [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]], that was spoken by the [[Pallanganmiddang people]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Blake |first=Barry |last2=Reid |first2=Julie |date=2002 |title=The Dhudhuroa language of northeastern Victoria: a description based on historical sources |url=https://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p73361/pdf/ch0844.pdf |journal=Aboriginal History |volume=26 |pages=177–210}}</ref>

== Name ==
Many tribe and language names in the area end in a suffix variously spelt {{lang|pmd|-matong}}, {{lang|pmd|-middang}}, {{lang|pmd|-mirttong}}, {{lang|pmd|-mathang}}, and {{lang|pmd|-mittung}};<ref name="Blake and Reid">{{cite journal |last1=Blake |first1=Barry J. |last2=Reid |first2=Julie |date=1999 |title=Pallanganmiddang: a language of the Upper Murray |journal=Aboriginal Languages |volume=23 |pages=15–31}}</ref>{{rp||pages=|page=2}} this suffix may have an etymological association with "speech" or "tongue" (compare Western Australian language [[Kalaamaya language|Kalaamaya's]] {{lang|lkm|midhany}} "tongue", likely a [[cognate]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Dhudhuroa Language of Northeastern Victoria: A Description Based on Historical Sources {{!}} I-Portal: Indigenous Studies Portal |url=https://iportal.usask.ca/record/40749 |access-date=2025-02-16 |website=iportal.usask.ca |page=179}}</ref>), and, in Pallanganmiddang's case, seems to denote an [[ethnonym]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Clark |first=Ian D |date=2009 |title=Dhudhuroa and Yaithmathang languages and social groups in north-east Victoria – a reconstruction |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24046829 |journal=Aboriginal History |volume=33 |page=210 |jstor=24046829 |issn=0314-8769}}</ref>

Pallanganmiddang has been alternatively known as Balangamida, Pallangahmiddang, Pal-ler an mitter, Wavaroo, Wave Veroo, Waveroo, Wayyourong, Wayyouroo, Wayerroo, Waywurru, Weeerroo and Weeherroo.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-03-21 |title=Pallanganmiddang {{!}} Ethnologue |url=https://www.ethnologue.com/language/pmd/ |access-date=2025-02-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130321073944/https://www.ethnologue.com/language/pmd/ |archive-date=21 March 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=ScriptSource - Pallanganmiddang |url=https://scriptsource.org/cms//scripts/page.php?item_id=language_detail&key=pmd |access-date=2025-02-19 |website=scriptsource.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eira |first=Christina |date=2008 |title=Not tigers – sisters! Advances in the interpretation of historical source spellings for |url=https://www.academia.edu/6647391 |journal=Aboriginal History |volume=32}}</ref>

== Classification ==
Although it was a [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama-Nyungan]] language,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Glottolog 5.1 - Pallanganmiddang |url=https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/pall1243 |access-date=2025-02-19 |website=glottolog.org}}</ref> Pallanganmiddang was evidently quite distinct from its neighbouring languages, such as [[Dhudhuroa language|Dhudhuroa]], [[Yorta Yorta language|Yorta Yorta]] and [[Wiradjuri language|Wiradjuri]]; its percentage of shared vocabulary with these neighbours is very low. The only exception is the language mentioned in an 1899 list titled "Barwidgee, Upper Murray", with which Pallanganmiddang shares 39% of its vocabulary. This source may actually show a dialect of [[Dhudhuroa language|Dhudhuroa]] spoken near the border of Pallanganmiddang territory, or it may be conflating two languages, although the list's use of words not native to the area suggests its lack of reliability.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=3}}

Despite its seeming lack of closeness to neighbouring languages, Pallanganmiddang does contain many [[Root (linguistics)|roots]] familiar in Aboriginal languages such as {{lang|pmd|nha-}} "to see", and {{lang|pmd|yan-}} "to go".<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=3}}

== Documentation ==
There are only four [[primary source]] documents on the language: a vocabulary of 46 words from 1878 and a vocabulary of 109 words from 1886, a vocabulary of 341 words of unclear date, and a vocabulary of 63 words from 1900, which, taken together, provide a list of more than 300 words.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=1–2}}

* The variation between ''p''/''b'', ''t''/''d'', and ''k''/''g'' in the sources suggest a lack of [[Phoneme|phonemic]] distinction between [[Voice (phonetics)|voiced and voiceless]] consonants.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=3}}
* There was probably not a phonemic distinction between dentals and palatals, since some words are recorded with both ''t''/''d,'' suggesting a [[Dental consonant|dental]] or [[Alveolar consonant|alveolar]] [[plosive]], ''and j/g,'' suggesting a [[Palatal consonant|palatal]] plosive (e.g. "foot" is variously spelt {{lang|pmd|teerrer}} or {{lang|pmd|gerra}}, "man" is variously spelt {{lang|pmd|teerre}}, {{lang|pmd|gerree}} or {{lang|pmd|jere}}).<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=3–4|page=}}
* There is no definite evidence for [[Retroflex consonant|retroflexes]], but the spelling of {{lang|pmd|carrda}} "crayfish" suggests they existed.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=4}}
* There probably was a distinction between a [[Tap and flap consonants|flapped]] or [[Trill consonant|trilled]] [[Rhotic consonant|rhotic]], and a glide-type rhotic (possibly a retroflex), but such distinctions were not made in older sources.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=4}}

=== Vowels ===
Pallanganmiddang may have had only three vowels /i/, /u/ and /a/, similar to many Aboriginal languages, although the exact amount is unclear. Nonetheless, according to different sources, ''a'', ''e'', ''i'', ''o'', and ''u'' are all used. There may have been a distinction between [[Vowel length|long and short]] vowels, as suggested by the spelling in the first syllable of {{lang|pmd|karmborro}} "group", but this is unclear.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=5}}

There may have been no phonemic distinction between ''u'' and ''o'', as suggested by variant spellings, such as {{lang|pmd|koro}} and {{lang|pmd|kurru}} "blood".<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=5}}

Monosyllabic words with no final consonant seemingly contained a long vowel (e.g. {{lang|pmd|mii}} "eye", {{lang|pmd|ngaa}} "nose"), a feature common in Aboriginal languages.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=6}}

== Grammar ==
No [[primary source]] data are available for Pallanganmiddang's grammar. However, there are short sentences included in the collected vocabulary lists, although it is difficult to glean much information from them.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=6}}

=== Pronouns ===
The forms {{lang|pmd|innar}} and {{lang|pmd|neibee}} are both recorded for "you". Another word, {{lang|pmd|ninna}}, although given as "I", could possibly be a variant of {{lang|pmd|innar}}. If spelled {{lang|pmd|ngina}} (as the initial [[Voiced velar nasal|velar nasal]] may have been unheard), it matches a word meaning "you" in [[Yorta Yorta]] and [[Latji-Latji language|Latji-Latji]].<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=6}}

{{lang|pmd|Itebe}} is recorded for "I". This could have been pronounced something like {{lang|pmd|ngaytbi}}, and so {{lang|pmd|neibee}}, although given as "you", could perhaps be a [[First person pronoun|first-person pronoun]]. In fact, {{lang|pmd|neibee}} seems to match the final two syllables in {{lang|pmd|bang(g)owonabi}} (translated as "hungry"), {{lang|pmd|waurranmandjianabi}} (translated as "thirsty") and {{lang|pmd|kanimanabi}} (translated as "drink"), possibly meaning "I'm hungry", "I'm thirsty", and "I drink".<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=6–7|page=}}

{{lang|pmd|Nyeende-nanga-durrah}} is recorded for "me", and {{lang|pmd|nyeende}} for "my". However, a velar nasal, rather than the implied [[Voiced palatal nasal|palatal nasal]] from the spelling, is more typical for first person pronouns in languages in the area. This could suggest they are possibly misglossed and are actually second person pronouns; alternatively, a sound change could have occurred, or the text could be erroneous.<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=7}}

One wordlist records {{lang|pmd|wowandowan}} for "hungry"; since ''wan'' means "I" in several other languages in Victoria, this possibly suggests a translation of {{lang|pmd|wowandowan}} as "I'm hungry" and therefore ''wan'' as a [[Bound and free morphemes|bound]] first-person pronoun (and the previously mentioned {{lang|pmd|ngina}}, etc. as the free form).<ref name="Blake and Reid" />{{rp||pages=|page=7}}
